newsitem.title: USA: Schwinn regains independence with Questor buyout.
newsitem.headline: Schwinn regains independence with Questor buyout.

text.p: Schwinn, the once-proud bicycle maker that has spent the past five years clawing its way out of bankruptcy, will become an independent company again with its purchase by Questor Partners Fund LP by from Scott Sports Group Inc.
Terms of the transaction, announced Wednesday, were not disclosed.

Questor, a Southfield-based investment group that buys underperforming companies, said it intends to retain Schwinn Cycling and Fitness Inc.'s Boulder, Colo., headquarters, its management and its 280 U.S. employees.

The deal marks the second change of hands for Schwinn since the former family-owned, Chicago-based company wobbled into bankruptcy in 1992. Although it was one of the best selling U.S. bicycle brands for much of this century, Schwinn failed to capitalize on the explosion of mountain bikes in the 1970s and '80s, allowing a host of competitors to rise to prominence.
Scott, majority-owned by the Zell-Chilmark Fund LP, paid $40.75 million for Schwinn in 1993 and moved its headquarters out to Boulder, a mountain biking mecca, to change its culture.
Since then, Schwinn has been working to rebuild its brand image with new products, notably a new line of high-end mountain and road bike frames and high-tech fitness equipment.

Kevin Keenley, vice president of Questor Partners, said Schwinn has returned to profitability, but Questor believes it can significantly improve the company's performance by instituting new business practices and production efficiencies.

"The Schwinn management has come a long way since the bankruptcy in 1992 and they've done a wonderful job of salvaging the Schwinn brand," he said. "We think it's time to take the whole turnaround to the next level."
Questor is headed by Jay Alix, a corporate turnaround expert who has worked to improve National Car Rental System Inc., Unisys Corp., Hartmarx Corp., and Cardinal Industries.

Other Questor principals include Dan Lufkin, co-founder of Donaldson, Lufkin & Jennrette Securities Corp. and former Transamerica Corp. president Edward Scarff. Questor's currrent holdings incldue consumer truck rental firm Ryder TRS Inc. in Denver and Tube Products Corp. of Vandalia, Ohio.

In addition to the Boulder headquarters, Questor is acquiring Schwinn distribution facilities in California, Illinois and New Jersey, as well as a factory in Durango, Colo., that builds Schwinn Homegrown and Yeti brand mountain bike frames. Most of Schwinn's bicycles, sold through 1,800 independent bike dealers, are built under contract overseas.
Sun Valley, Idaho-based Scott, best known for its ski equipment, will retain its own brand of mountain bikes.

"Questor is the perfect financial partner for Schwinn," said Scott Chairman Chuck Ferries. "We will work closely with Questor to make sure there is a smooth transition for both the Schwinn and Scott brands."
In addition to developing a new family of mountain and road bikes, Schwinn also hopes to cash in on the nostalgia of baby boomers who rode its products in the 1950s and '60s.

It recently brought out a $3,000 limited reproduction of its 1950 Black Phantom model, and also is looking at resurrecting some of its other classic brands, such as the Sting-Ray. It plans to reintroduce its Paramount brand of road bicycles later this year, said Greg Bagni, vice president of marketing.
